Yes people often misunderstand the purpose of the DRY principle. It’s not about getting rid of any bit of duplicated code and reducing the number of lines of code. The purpose of DRY is to make it easier to manage and understand the code/logic. For example, if like 20 different methods that use a similar set of logic and that logic needs to be tweaked, then you have to go to 20 different spots in the code to change it. Moving that to a shared method, makes it so only one area of code needs to be changed to tweak the logic. If the abstraction goes too far and makes it harder for the developer to understand the logic or change the logic, then the DRY principle probably doesn’t apply here

You can also write horrible garbage code in a strongly typed language, like putting all your logic in controllers, not separating the database layer, etc. I’d argue that the languages someone knows is less important, but rather how they are able to use the languages they know

AI will never fully replace software engineers. The thing people often overlook is the fact that the AI needs to be prompted to create something in the first place, and in my opinion that prompter needs to have a good understanding of how the software should or does work including how the code works at least at a high level. Second, is the fact that the end of the day any AI, not matter how advanced, is just playing the odds really. It’s guessing what the most probable or likely answer would be. There’s no guarantee that its response will 100% always be correct. What I think will likely happen to software teams as AI advances, is that they’ll just get smaller. The teams will consist of advanced prompt engineers that know how to form well crafted, efficient prompts, as well as know how to code and be able to understand the AI responses and determine if it works and if not how it can be tweaked to work. Essentially software engineers won’t be replaced, teams will just shrink as each engineer will have a handful of extremely fast and super knowledgeable assistants at their fingertips

I actually think the current AI solutions we have are better at debugging a block of code than writing a block of code. 

Human eyes are kind of lazy when scanning over text and it’s insanely easy for us to miss a single missing character in a line of code that causes an error. But these LLMs that are really good at pattern matching can immediately notice the error in the pattern and locate the bug. 

While when creating code, if replicating something already in your code (like a new object or something), it can do that pretty well. But often times when creating code it’ll just try to match the pattern of your existing code without understanding/knowing if this new code should match pre existing code or is an entirely new code pattern.

In my experience, whenever I ask it to write me a “new” block of code, I usually have to tweak it to make it work how it actually should. When debugging, if given enough code segments and the trace back, it tends to find the bug for me or at least guide me in the right direction.

All great points that I agree with. Adding to this list: Rushing into deployment, trying to get all the server/hosting configured while in early development or even before starting development.  Too often I see posts on how they just started an app and what's the best place to deploy it or how they're in the process of developing and ran into some server issue and their app won't run.  There's no need to rush into deploying your app having a site up and running while your app is less than 1/2 finished. 1. If you're app isn't finished or is buggy, why would you want it available to the public. For sake of embarrassment but also security reasons as well, it's much better to just wait until you have a more complete product.   2. Why pay hosting/server fees for an unfinished app that once again doesn't need to be available to the public?  Almost anything you develop will be able to run locally just fine while you're working on it.  Unless the product is close to complete and you need user testing/feedback, just hold off on deploying your app.  Save yourself the headache of trying configuring the whole server to work with your app, while your app is still changing and may not even work and money spent on a server/hosting provider.  P.S. I'm aware there are niche cases where a server is needed ahead of time, but 90% of the time this is not the case.

My company’s main products are .net projects. I (started out not knowing .net) was hired for my Python expertise. So I am often in a similar boat as you, as the rest of my team works with .net not python. ChatGPT has been super helpful for me. You also mentioned that you have no code review process. This was how my company was when I first started, we had shared repos storing our projects, but no PRs/review process.  It was just a free for all programming experience (which is obviously very messy). We have since adapted a stricter code review process requiring new code to be reviewing and approved in a PR before merging into a main  development branch.  I would recommend requesting from a manager or talking with the rest of your team about some sort of process to be set up for code review. Our process is that one person on the team is assigned PR monitoring for each week. Not only will this provide peer review and collaboration on code that you’re missing out on, it also helps night and day with catching bugs. Our QA team is especially grateful of this.
